d: The amount the GP aims to raise, stated in the PPM. It should come from the portfolio construction model, the number and size of deals the team can execute, and the fee income needed to run the business.
x: A €150m target based on 25 initial cheques of €3m plus 50% reserves.
A ₹400 crore target for a Cat II credit fund.
s: The team sets €300m because a peer did.
LPs test the number against the portfolio model and the team's capacity; an oversized target signals poor discipline.
Fundraising stalls at 60% of target.
The GP can close smaller if the LPA allows, adjusting portfolio construction.

d: The maximum fund size the LPA permits. Commitments above it are refused. A hard cap protects LPs from strategy drift caused by too much capital.
x: Target €150m, hard cap €200m.
A hard cap set at 1.25x target.
s: Demand reaches €260m against a €200m cap.
The GP scales back allocations, often favouring existing LPs.
The GP wants to lift the cap.
An LPA amendment needs LP consent.

d: The amount an LP legally agrees to contribute over the fund's life. It is not paid upfront; the GP calls it in instalments as needed, usually over four to six years.
x: An LP commits €10m; by year 3, €6m has been called.
A ₹5 crore commitment to an Indian AIF drawn in five tranches.
s: An LP's liquidity tightens.
It must still meet calls up to its commitment or face default remedies.
The fund invests only 85% of commitments.
The rest stays uncalled; LPs never pay it.

d: The team's prior investment results, usually shown deal by deal with gross and net returns, dates and cash flows. The main thing LPs diligence, along with whether the people who made those returns are still on the team.
x: A deal-by-deal table with entry, exit, MOIC and IRR for 18 investments.
Attribution of returns from a partner's time at a previous firm.
s: A partner claims a deal led by a colleague.
LP reference checks expose it; credibility suffers across the whole raise.
Prior fund returns rely on one outlier.
LPs look at returns excluding the top deal to judge repeatability.

d: A fund raised by a team without a prior fund under the same brand. LPs look harder at attributable track record, team stability, alignment and operational set-up, and often ask for better terms.
x: A €60m Fund I raised mostly from family offices and angels.
An emerging manager programme at a pension fund backing three Fund Is.
s: Institutional LPs decline because the fund is under their minimum size.
The team targets family offices, funds of funds and emerging manager programmes.
An anchor offers 30% of target for GP economics.
The team weighs the share of carry against faster fundraising.

d: Testing investor interest in a fund before it is available to subscribe. EU rules allow it with conditions: no final documents, no subscription possible, notice to the home regulator within two weeks. Subscriptions within 18 months count as marketing.
x: Sharing draft terms with ten EU institutions to test appetite.
A notified pre-marketing round in Germany and the Netherlands.
s: An LP contacted in pre-marketing subscribes a year later claiming reverse solicitation.
Within 18 months it counts as marketing; the fund must have been notified for that country.
A deck includes a signable subscription form.
That is marketing, not pre-marketing.

d: An LP's non-binding indication that it plans to commit a given amount, used to gauge momentum before a close.
x: €40m soft-circled toward a €100m first close.
An LP soft-circling pending investment committee approval.
s: Soft circles total 80% of target but only half convert.
Teams track conversion rates rather than counting soft circles as money.
An LP withdraws its soft circle.
No legal consequence; it was non-binding.

d: The first date commitments are accepted and the fund starts operating. Investing and management fees usually start here.
x: First close at 50% of target after nine months.
A SEBI scheme's first close after meeting the ₹20 crore minimum corpus.
s: The GP wants to close at 25% of target.
Too small a first close may not support portfolio construction; LPs may wait.
A deal is ready before first close.
It may be warehoused and transferred to the fund after closing.

d: Any close after the first at which further LPs are admitted, up to the final close. Later LPs pay equalisation.
x: Second close three months after first close.
Four closings over 14 months.
s: A new LP joins after two investments.
It pays its share of called capital plus interest.
Earlier LPs object to late investors joining.
Late-closing interest compensates them.

d: The last date new commitments are accepted. LPAs usually require it within 12 to 18 months of first close.
x: Final close at €180m, 14 months after first close.
Final close extended by three months with LPAC consent.
s: A large LP needs two more months.
The GP seeks an extension if the LPA allows.
The fund is below target at the deadline.
It closes at the amount raised.

d: The window from launch to final close. Market data show it lengthened in 2023–2025, with many funds taking more than 18 months from first marketing to final close.
x: A 20-month raise for a Fund II.
A Fund I taking 30 months.
s: The raise runs long.
Partners split time between fundraising and investing; LPs notice.
Fee start date and the long raise.
Fees often run from first close, so late LPs pay equalised fees.

d: Demand exceeding the hard cap or target. The GP allocates, cutting back new LPs or large tickets, and may use the strength to tighten terms.
x: €300m of demand for a €200m hard cap.
An LP allocated €12m against a €20m request.
s: Existing LPs and new LPs both want in.
Most GPs prioritise re-ups to reward loyalty.
The GP is tempted to raise the cap.
Larger funds can push the team into bigger deals outside its edge.

d: The smallest commitment the fund accepts, set by the GP and sometimes by regulation (₹1 crore for SEBI AIFs, USD 250,000 for IFSCA venture schemes).
x: €5m minimum for an institutional buyout fund, waivable by the GP.
₹1 crore minimum under SEBI rules.
s: An angel offers €100,000 to a fund with a €1m minimum.
The GP may waive the fund's own minimum, but not a regulatory one.
An Indian accredited investor offers ₹50 lakh.
Accredited investors are exempt from the ₹1 crore minimum.

d: LPs admitted at later closes pay their share of capital already called, plus an interest charge, so that every LP ends up as if it had joined at first close. Earlier LPs get the excess back.
x: Late-closing interest at a fixed rate such as 8% a year.
An equalisation payment of €1.2m from a new LP.
s: A deal is marked up before the new LP joins.
The new LP pays cost plus interest, not the marked-up value; earlier LPs keep part of the upside.
Interest rate set too low.
Late LPs get a cheap option; LPs push for market-rate interest.

a: GP commit, skin in the game
d: Capital the GP and team invest in their own fund on the same terms as LPs. LPs read it as the clearest sign of alignment, and check whether it is paid in cash or through fee waivers.
x: Commonly 1–2% of commitments in PE; often 1% in VC.
A team committing 3% personally.
s: The GP proposes funding its commitment by waiving fees.
Some LPs accept; others insist on cash. SEBI does not accept waivers for continuing interest.
A partner leaves.
Their share of GP commitment is usually transferred to remaining partners.

d: India's rule on sponsor or manager skin in the game. Cat I and II: the lower of 2.5% of corpus or ₹5 crore. Cat III: the lower of 5% or ₹10 crore. It cannot be met by waiving fees. Angel funds use a per-deal rule.
x: ₹5 crore for a ₹300 crore Cat II fund (2.5% would be ₹7.5 crore).
5% of a ₹100 crore Cat III fund = ₹5 crore.
s: The fund grows from ₹100 crore to ₹250 crore.
Continuing interest must keep pace pro rata to funds raised, capped at the regulatory amount.
The sponsor offers a fee waiver instead.
Not permitted.

d: Each scheme of an Indian AIF needs a corpus of at least ₹20 crore, or ₹10 crore for angel funds, before it can begin operating.
x: A ₹20 crore first close for a Cat I scheme.
A ₹10 crore angel fund.
s: The scheme has ₹15 crore of commitments.
It cannot hold first close yet.
Corpus counts commitments, not paid-in capital.
Commitments signed by investors count toward the threshold.

d: An Indian AIF cannot accept less than ₹1 crore from an investor, or ₹25 lakh from employees and directors of the manager or sponsor. Accredited investors are exempt.
x: A ₹1 crore commitment from an HNI.
A ₹25 lakh commitment from a manager employee.
s: Two spouses want to invest ₹50 lakh each.
Joint investment rules allow up to two persons jointly to meet the ₹1 crore threshold.
An accredited investor offers ₹40 lakh.
Allowed.

d: An investor certified as meeting wealth or income thresholds, and so able to access products with fewer protections. India runs an accreditation regime through accreditation agencies; the US uses the Regulation D definition.
x: An Indian family trust accredited through a depository-linked agency.
A US individual with over $1m net worth excluding primary residence.
s: An accredited Indian investor wants a smaller ticket.
Exempt from the ₹1 crore minimum.
A US 506(c) offering.
Every investor must be verified as accredited.

d: Under MiFID II, investors such as banks, insurers, pension funds and large companies, plus individuals who opt up and meet tests. AIFMD marketing passports cover professional investors only.
x: A German insurer as a per se professional client.
A wealthy individual opting up after meeting trading and portfolio criteria.
s: A retail client asks to invest in a RAIF.
Only if they qualify as well-informed; the passport covers professionals.
An individual opts up.
The distributor documents the assessment.

d: Luxembourg's eligibility category for RAIFs and SIFs: institutional or professional investors, or others who confirm in writing and invest at least €100,000 or are assessed by a bank or investment firm.
x: An entrepreneur investing €150,000 in a RAIF.
A family office assessed by its bank.
s: An investor offers €80,000.
Needs a positive expertise assessment to qualify.
The fund relies on assessments.
Documentation must be kept for the regulator.

d: US category for 3(c)(7) funds: individuals with at least $5m in investments, and entities with at least $25m, among others. 3(c)(7) funds have no 100-investor limit.
x: A US family office with $40m investments.
A 3(c)(7) fund with 400 investors.
s: A fund nears 100 investors under 3(c)(1).
Switching to 3(c)(7) requires all investors to be qualified purchasers.
An investor has $3m of investments.
Not a qualified purchaser.

d: The make-up of the fund's investors by type and country. A diversified, institutional base helps future fundraising and reduces default risk; concentration in one LP creates dependence.
x: A Fund I with 60% family offices and 40% institutions.
A Fund III with 30% re-ups from sovereign funds.
s: One LP holds 40% of the fund.
Its votes can swing consents; key person and removal clauses matter more.
A fund has many small HNIs.
Administration and KYC costs rise; defaults are more likely.

a: seed investor, GP stake at launch
d: A seed investor provides capital to a new manager, sometimes funding the fund and the management company, in exchange for a share of revenue or carry. Common for first-time managers.
x: A seeder committing $50m for 15% of the manager's revenue.
A family office funding ManCo costs for two years for a carry share.
s: A seeder's revenue share lasts forever.
Teams negotiate sunsets or buy-back rights.
LPs ask about GP economics.
Seed arrangements must be disclosed in diligence.

d: The GP or a third party buys investments before the fund's first close and transfers them to the fund later, usually at cost plus a carrying charge. It lets the fund start with a portfolio LPs can see.
x: Two deals warehoused by the GP and moved into the fund at first close.
A bank warehouse facility holding assets for a new infrastructure fund.
s: A warehoused deal doubles in value before transfer.
LPs get the asset at cost plus interest; the conflict is disclosed and consented.
A warehoused deal falls in value.
If transfer is at cost, LPs overpay; LPAs often allow opting out or require fair value.

d: An authorised EU AIFM can market an EU AIF to professional investors across the EU after notifying its home regulator, without separate approval in each country.
x: A Luxembourg AIFM passporting a RAIF into France and Germany.
A notification processed within 20 working days.
s: The fund wants retail investors abroad.
The passport covers professionals; retail needs ELTIF or national rules.
The manager is outside the EU.
No passport; national private placement instead.

d: Country-by-country rules for marketing funds that cannot use the passport, such as non-EU funds, into individual EU states and the UK. Conditions and fees vary; some countries ban it.
x: A Cayman fund registered for NPPR in the Netherlands and Sweden.
A US manager filing NPPR in the UK.
s: A target country does not allow NPPR.
The manager uses a Luxembourg parallel fund with a host AIFM.
NPPR filings lapse.
Further marketing in that country stops until refiled.

d: An investor approaches the manager on its own initiative, outside marketing rules. A narrow exception: the EU blocks it for 18 months after pre-marketing, and Monaco prohibits unlicensed firms from canvassing residents even when solicited.
x: An EU pension fund contacting a US manager unprompted.
A Monaco resident emailing a foreign manager directly.
s: A manager holds a webinar, then relies on reverse solicitation.
Regulators treat this as marketing.
A Monaco family asks a Swiss manager for documents.
Without CCAF authorisation, providing services may breach Monaco law.

d: A request for LPs to pay part of their unfunded commitment, used to fund investments, fees and expenses. Calls follow the LPA notice period and are pro rata to commitments.
x: A 6% call to fund a new investment and quarterly fees.
A call bundled quarterly after a subscription line funded deals.
s: A deal closes in five days but notice is ten business days.
The fund draws on a subscription line and calls capital later.
Calls come faster than expected.
LPs adjust liquidity plans; pacing models are updated.

d: Total capital LPs have contributed to date. The denominator for DPI, RVPI and TVPI.
x: €60m paid in on €100m of commitments.
Paid-in including fees and expenses.
s: A sub line delays calls.
Paid-in stays lower for longer, which flatters early multiples and IRR.
Recallable distributions are re-called.
Paid-in increases by the re-called amount.

d: Commitment an LP has made but the GP has not yet called. It stays a legal obligation until the investment period ends or the fund is wound up, so LPs have to keep liquidity aside for it. Summed across the industry it is called dry powder.
x: €25m unfunded on a €100m fund in year 5.
Global private equity dry powder measured by data providers.
s: An LP sells its interest.
The buyer takes on the unfunded obligation too.
A fund ends its investment period with 20% unfunded.
Calls continue only for follow-ons, fees and expenses.

d: The window, usually four to six years from first close, in which the fund may make new investments. Afterwards it can only make follow-ons, pay expenses and complete deals already agreed.
x: A five-year investment period ending early if 90% is committed.
An investment period suspended by a key person event.
s: The fund is 90% deployed in year 3.
Many LPAs end the investment period early once a successor fund is raised or capital is committed.
A great deal appears after the period ends.
The fund cannot take it as a new investment.

d: The years after the investment period when the team manages and sells the portfolio. Fees usually fall to an invested-capital basis.
x: Years 6–10 of a 10-year fund.
A harvest period with three exits a year.
s: Exit markets close in year 7.
The GP may seek extensions or secondaries.
Fees drop as the portfolio shrinks.
Team economics shift to carry.

d: The fund's contractual life, typically ten years from first close for PE and VC, plus extensions.
x: 10 years plus two one-year extensions.
A SEBI Cat II scheme with a 7-year tenure.
s: Assets remain at year 10.
Extensions, secondaries or in-kind distribution follow.
LPs want a shorter term.
Shorter terms suit credit; equity needs longer.

d: Extra time beyond the fund term to finish exits. Often two one-year extensions, the first at GP discretion and the second with LPAC or LP consent. SEBI allows up to two years with two-thirds investor approval for close-ended Cat I/II schemes.
x: A first extension at GP discretion; second with LPAC consent.
A SEBI scheme extended by two years with investor vote.
s: The GP seeks a third extension.
Not allowed under most LPAs; GP-led secondaries become an option.
LPs consent to extend.
They often require reduced fees.

d: Reinvesting proceeds from early exits instead of distributing them, within a cap in the LPA. It lets the fund invest close to 100% of commitments despite fees.
x: Recycling allowed until 120% of commitments has been invested.
Recycling of proceeds from exits within 18 months of investment.
s: A deal exits in year 2 for 1.2x.
Proceeds may be recycled into new deals rather than distributed.
LPs want cash back.
Recycling caps protect LPs from indefinite reinvestment.

d: A distribution that the GP may call again later, adding it back to unfunded commitments. Used for early returns of capital, bridge repayments and recycling.
x: Proceeds of a quick flip marked as recallable.
Return of unused capital called for a deal that fell through.
s: An LP treats a recallable distribution as final.
It may face a later call; liquidity planning should keep it.
The LPA limits recall to 12 months.
After that the distribution becomes final.

d: Part of the fund held back for later rounds in companies already in the portfolio, so the fund can defend its ownership and support winners. Venture funds commonly reserve 30–60% of capital; reserving too little leads to dilution, too much leaves money idle.
x: Seed funds often reserve 40–60% of the fund.
A buyout fund reserving 10% for add-on acquisitions.
s: A company's next round prices high.
The fund decides whether reserves are best spent there or elsewhere.
Reserves run out.
The fund is diluted or uses an annex fund.

d: How quickly the fund commits and invests capital. Too fast concentrates the portfolio in one market moment; too slow delays returns.
x: 25% of commitments invested per year.
A fund fully deployed in 2021 at peak valuations.
s: Valuations peak.
Disciplined funds slow deployment; LPs compare pace to plan.
The fund is slow.
Fees on committed capital raise fee drag.

d: The return lost when capital sits uninvested. For LPs it comes from holding cash for future calls; for open-ended funds, from liquidity sleeves.
x: An LP holding 30% of commitments in cash for calls.
An evergreen fund with a 15% liquid sleeve.
s: An LP overcommits to reduce drag.
It risks a liquidity squeeze if calls come faster.
An evergreen fund's sleeve earns money-market rates.
Total return lags the private portfolio.

d: Cash or securities paid out to partners, usually after an exit or income receipt, allocated through the waterfall.
x: €20m distributed after a trade sale.
Quarterly income distributions from a credit fund.
s: Part of the distribution goes to carry.
LPs receive their share after the waterfall.
Tax is withheld.
Net amount reaches the LP.

d: Distributing shares rather than cash, most often listed shares after an IPO lock-up ends. SEBI requires in-specie distribution of unsold assets at the end of the dissolution period.
x: Listed shares distributed to LPs post-IPO.
An Indian scheme distributing unlisted shares in specie at dissolution.
s: LPs receive shares they cannot hold.
They sell immediately or appoint a broker; price may fall.
Valuation for carry purposes.
The LPA sets the price used, often a VWAP.

d: A distribution to the GP or partners to cover tax on allocated income before cash proceeds arrive, common in US funds where partners are taxed on income as it is allocated.
x: A distribution to the GP to pay tax on allocated carry gains.
A tax distribution advanced against future carry.
s: Carry allocated but not paid in cash.
A tax distribution prevents the GP paying tax out of pocket.
Later the GP owes clawback.
Clawback is usually limited to after-tax amounts.

d: An LP who fails to meet a capital call. LPA remedies include default interest, suspension of rights, forced sale of the interest at a discount and forfeiture.
x: An LP forced to sell its interest at 50% of NAV after default.
Default interest at 10% a year.
s: An LP misses a call by two days.
Cure periods usually allow late payment with interest.
An LP refuses to pay.
Other LPs may be called to cover the shortfall within caps.

d: An LP's right not to fund a particular investment for legal, regulatory or policy reasons, such as a ban on tobacco or weapons.
x: A Shariah-compliant LP excused from a conventional lender.
A public pension excused from a gambling company.
s: An LP is excused.
Others fund its share within concentration limits.
Excuse claimed for performance reasons.
Not allowed; excuse is for legal or policy grounds.

d: A bank facility secured on LPs' uncalled commitments. The fund borrows to invest quickly and calls capital later, which smooths calls but raises reported IRR. ILPA guidance asks for disclosure of returns with and without the facility.
x: Calls bundled quarterly while the facility funds deals in between.
A 90-day repayment requirement.
s: IRR rises from 14% to 18% due to the facility.
LPs ask for IRR excluding the facility.
Rates rise.
Interest cost reduces net returns; GPs shorten usage.

d: A loan to the fund secured on the value of its portfolio, used later in fund life for follow-ons, liquidity or early distributions. Controversial when used to fund distributions.
x: A $100m NAV loan at 15% loan-to-value.
A NAV facility funding follow-ons in year 7.
s: The GP borrows to distribute and boost DPI.
LPs may object; the loan adds risk to remaining assets.
Portfolio values fall.
LTV covenants may force asset sales.

d: LPA cap on fund-level borrowing and guarantees, usually a percentage of commitments and time limit. Regulators may add limits, for example SEBI's restrictions on Cat I/II borrowing.
x: Borrowing capped at 20% of commitments for up to 12 months.
Guarantees of portfolio company debt prohibited.
s: The GP wants a large facility.
It must stay within the cap or seek consent.
Borrowing exceeds 12 months.
Breach; LPs may require repayment.

d: Cash held back from distributions to pay future fund expenses and contingent liabilities, especially near the end of the fund.
x: €2m held back for warranty claims after a sale.
Reserves for audit and liquidation costs.
s: Reserves are larger than needed.
Excess is distributed at wind-up.
SEBI scheme retains reserves after fund life.
Allowed only in defined circumstances under the 2026 rules.

d: The obligation of LPs to return distributions to cover fund liabilities, such as indemnities, arising after distribution. Usually capped (for example 25% of distributions) and time-limited.
x: Giveback capped at 25% of distributions for two years.
A giveback call to fund a warranty claim.
s: A buyer claims warranties after the fund distributed proceeds.
The GP calls giveback within the LPA cap.
Giveback period expires.
LPs are no longer liable.

d: A vehicle that holds the fund's remaining assets or claims after dissolution so the fund can close while residual matters are resolved.
x: A liquidating trust holding an escrow receivable.
A trust pursuing litigation on behalf of former LPs.
s: An earn-out is due in two years.
The trust holds the right and distributes when paid.
LPs want to close their books.
The trust allows the fund to dissolve.

d: The end of the fund: remaining assets sold or distributed, liabilities settled, final accounts audited and the vehicle dissolved. In India a one-year liquidation period follows tenure, with an optional dissolution period.
x: A fund liquidated in year 12.
A SEBI scheme surrendering registration.
s: One asset remains unsold.
Options are in-kind distribution, a liquidating trust or a continuation vehicle.
Pending litigation.
Reserves are kept; SEBI's 2026 rules allow retention in defined cases.
